<meta>This page contains commentaries on verses 37, 38, and 39 of the fifth chapter of the Manusmṛti, focusing on the regulations regarding animal slaughter and the ritual substitution of animals.</meta>

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** Even when there is an extremely intense craving <term>rāga</term> <gloss>passion or desire</gloss> for eating meat, one’s desire should be satisfied by other means; it is not proper to commit animal violence <term>paśu-hiṃsā</term>. He says, "he should make." A "ghee-animal" <note>an effigy made of clarified butter</note> is a transformation of ghee, called an "animal" because it takes the form of animal meat. Similarly, one may use a "flour-animal" <note>an effigy made of dough</note>. "In association" <term>saṅge</term> refers to extreme desire. Some interpret "association" as being overcome by spirits or similar influences, but this is not supported by common worldly usage. || 37 ||

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** If there is "association" <term>saṅge</term> <gloss>attachment</gloss>, meaning a fondness for eating meat, one should make an image of an animal out of ghee or flour and eat that. However, one should never wish to kill animals without the intention of offering them to a deity. || 37 ||

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** A "ghee-animal" is a replica of an animal made of ghee. "In association" means when one is attached to animal sacrifice or has a passionate desire for eating. This applies to necessary domestic rituals <term>smārta-karma</term> but not to Vedic rituals <term>vaidika-karma</term>, because in Vedic rites, using a ghee-animal would interfere with the specific rules of the eleven portions <note>the technical requirements of certain Vedic sacrifices</note>. Therefore, it is said that "killing in a sacrifice is not killing." || 37 ||

( 5 ) **Nandana:** He says "he should make" to show that one should not commit violence against the rules. "In association" means when people are gathered for a festival or meeting of kinsmen. In such cases, one should prepare a ghee-animal. In place of a living animal, one should offer plenty of ghee and flour-cakes <term>apūpa</term>. || 37 ||

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** One should make a ghee-animal when there is "association" <gloss>attachment</gloss>. One should likewise make a flour-animal. One should never desire to kill an animal in vain <term>vṛthā</term> <gloss>without ritual necessity</gloss>. || 37 ||

### As many hairs as there are on the animal, so many times does the vain animal-killer suffer death in birth after birth in the afterlife. || 38 ||

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** He undergoes the cycle of death for that many births. A "vain animal-killer" is one who performs animal slaughter not enjoined by the Vedas <term>Śruti</term> or the Law-books <term>Smṛti</term>. This refers to the context of hunters and others who kill for worldly purposes. The form "animal-killer" <term>paśughna</term> is a Vedic grammatical variation. || 38 ||

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** "So many times" means that specific number of times. A "vain animal-killer" is one who kills animals not authorized by the Vedas or Law-books. || 38 ||

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** One who kills animals for their own sake, without a purpose intended for the deities, is known as a "vain animal-killer." After death, they suffer being killed in as many future births as there are hairs on the animal. Therefore, one should not kill an animal in vain. The word "times" <term>kṛtvaḥ</term> is used to count the repetition of the action. The particle <term>ha</term> is used here to indicate that this is a well-known tradition from the sacred texts. || 38 ||

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** He describes the punishment for the opposite view <note>for those who kill outside of ritual</note> in this verse beginning with "As many." Here, the particle <term>ha</term> illuminates a well-known fact. || 38 ||

( 5 ) **Nandana:** "So many times" means that many instances. The particle <term>ha</term> is used here to express compassion. || 38 ||

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** A man who is a "vain animal-killer" commits an act of unrighteousness <term>adharma</term> in this world through killing. He attains the state of being an animal in the afterlife for as many times as there are hairs on the animal <note>said to be eighty million hairs</note> in birth after birth. || 38 ||

### Animals were created by the Self-Existent One <term>Svayambhū</term> <gloss>Brahmā</gloss> Himself for the sake of sacrifice, for the prosperity of this entire universe; therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not considered killing. || 39 ||

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** The fault mentioned previously does not apply here. Animals were produced by the Self-Existent One, Prajāpati, specifically to fulfill the prosperity that comes from slaughter enjoined by the Vedas and Law-books as part of a sacrifice. "Himself" is used for emphasis. Sacrifice, such as the <term>Jyotiṣṭoma</term>, is for the "prosperity" of this world. "Prosperity" means power, nourishment, and abundance. Therefore, the killing that occurs there should be understood as "non-killing." This is said because the sin arising from violence is removed in this context. || 39 ||

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** He removes the doubt regarding why there is no such fault in killing for sacrifice. It is for the "prosperity" or birth of the world. Through the oblations, the sun is nourished, leading to rain, then seeds, then semen, and finally the birth of living beings. By this, it is said that there is no fault, because through the death of one animal, many living beings are sustained. || 39 ||

---
<note>Footnote: Verse 38 variant: "tāvatkṛtvo ha" is written as "kṛtveha" in manuscripts Ka, Kha, Ga, Ṇa, and Ca.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the prohibition of killing animals for personal consumption and the merit of using ghee or flour effigies as substitutes. It explains that ritual slaughter for sacrifice is divinely ordained for the world's benefit and does not carry the karmic penalty of "vain" killing.</summary>
<keywords>animal sacrifice, substitution, ghee animal, flour animal, karma, ritual slaughter, Medhatithi, Kulluka, Manu, non-violence</keywords>
